summary:
ARES (Adaptive Route & Environment System) is an interactive 3D Mars map that plans safe routes for rovers and astronauts.

Signals between Earth and Mars take 3 to 22 minutes one way, so routes must be planned in advance using slope, temperature, geology and communication coverage, which normally sit in separate maps. ARES brings them together in one 3D view with five switchable layers (Terrain, Hazards, Thermal, Geology, Comms) and four regions (Gale, Jezero, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris).

Users click a destination and ARES computes a route using A* pathfinding in three modes: safest, shortest, or safe with continuous communication. It also offers a science tour, a dust-storm scenario, and four sensor panels modelled on NASA’s HiRISE, MOLA/HRSC, Mars Climate Sounder and CRISM data. Its distinctive feature is communication-aware routing, which avoids places where terrain blocks the line of sight to Earth.

The prototype uses simulated terrain and can import real elevation data from NASA Mars Trek. It is bilingual (Arabic and English).

ARES: Project Details

I could not open the official form, so these cover the fields Space Apps submissions usually ask for. Copy the ones that match your form.

What it does

ARES is an interactive 3D Mars map that plans safe routes for rovers and future astronauts. It combines terrain, hazards, temperature, geology and Earth-communication coverage in one view, so a planner can choose a destination and see a route, its distance, duration, maximum slope, estimated energy use and the share of the route without a direct link to Earth.

What we hoped to achieve

  • Turn scattered Mars data into one clear decision: where is it safe to go?
  • Make route planning understandable for students, planners and non-experts.
  • Build a prototype that real NASA data can replace without redesigning it.

How it works

  1. Terrain: a 96×96 elevation grid is rendered as a rotatable 3D surface with three.js.
  2. Analysis: slope is computed for each cell, and cells steeper than 28° are marked forbidden. Temperature depends on sun angle and elevation. Geology zones are assigned by location. Line of sight toward Earth is checked by tracing a ray over the terrain.
  3. Routing: an A* search finds a route in three modes: safest, shortest, or safe with continuous communication.
  4. Scenarios: a time-of-day slider, a dust-storm toggle, and a science tour across three targets.
  5. Sensor panels: optical, terrain, climate and mineral readings are computed from the current map.

What makes it different

  • Communication-aware routing: it avoids places where terrain blocks the line of sight to Earth. To our knowledge this is uncommon in similar prototypes, but we have not surveyed them.
  • Four regions: Gale, Jezero, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris, each with different terrain.
  • Bilingual interface in Arabic and English.

Tools and technologies

  • three.js (WebGL) for 3D rendering
  • A* pathfinding with a binary heap
  • Fractal noise for terrain generation
  • Ray tracing over a heightmap for communication shadows
  • A single HTML file, with no server or installation

Use of NASA data and technology

  • The sensor panels are modelled on NASA instruments: HiRISE (optical), MOLA and HRSC (elevation), Mars Climate Sounder (climate) and CRISM (minerals).
  • A DEM import button loads a grayscale elevation image, for example one exported from NASA Mars Trek, and rebuilds the slopes, route and sensor readings from it.
  • The prototype currently runs on simulated terrain. Claim "tested with real NASA data" only if you import a real DEM before submitting.

Limitations

  • The terrain, mineral zones, temperature and communication model are simplified. The Earth direction is fixed rather than computed from orbits.
  • Assumptions: 28° slope limit, 50 m cells, 0.1 km/h rover speed. Energy and solar figures are estimates.
  • It is an educational prototype and not flight software.

Future work

  • Real NASA Mars Trek tiles and DEM layers (in progress)
  • Dust-storm forecasting from climate data
  • AI hazard detection from rover images
  • A rover swarm with relay satellites
  • Resource maps for astronauts: buried ice, water and lower radiation
  • AR/VR view and an offline mission pack

Impact

ARES shows how open Mars data can support safer mission planning and make that planning easier to understand and teach.
